Moving block bootstrap for time-series statistics

Source: R/bootstrap.R
block_bootstrap.Rd

Puts uncertainty intervals on anything computed from a weekly panel (coefficients, contributions, average or marginal ROI) by resampling blocks of consecutive rows, refitting, and recomputing. Resampling single rows would destroy the autocorrelation that carryover creates and make the intervals too narrow; resampling blocks keeps it within each block (Künsch, 1989).

Usage

block_bootstrap(
  data,
  statistic,
  times = 200L,
  block_length = NULL,
  by = NULL,
  level = 0.9,
  seed = NULL,
  panel = c("shared", "independent"),
  index = NULL,
  circular = FALSE,
  cores = 1L
)

Arguments

data

A data frame, rows in time order (within each group when by is supplied), unless index names a column to order them by. It should hold everything statistic needs: typically the KPI, the transformed media, the controls and the raw spend.

statistic

A function of one data frame returning a named numeric vector. It is called once on data for the point estimate and once per replicate on a resampled copy. Replicates are matched to the estimate by name, so the order of the elements may change between calls; a replicate that returns a name the estimate does not have counts as failed, and a name it leaves out is missing for that replicate.

times

Number of bootstrap replicates, at most 1,000,000.

block_length

Rows per block, or periods per block when by is supplied with panel = "shared". The default, ceiling(n^(1/3)) with n the number of rows of data, is the usual rate-optimal order for the moving block bootstrap. It is often too short for media data; see "Choosing the block length".

by

Optional character vector of grouping columns, for a panel such as one series per geography. How the groups are resampled is set by panel.

level

Confidence level of the percentile intervals.

seed

Optional random seed, one whole number, for reproducible intervals. Every replicate's rows are drawn and the point estimate is computed after seeding, and the caller's random number stream is restored afterwards. Each replicate's call to statistic starts from a seed of its own, drawn before any replicate is evaluated, so a statistic that draws random numbers is reproducible too.

panel

How groups are resampled when by is supplied. "shared", the default, draws one set of blocks of periods and applies it to every group, so a shock that hit every geography in the same week stays together in each replicate. "independent" draws separate blocks for each group. That treats the groups as unrelated series, and for a statistic pooled across groups it gives intervals that are too narrow whenever the groups share shocks.

index

Optional name of a numeric, Date or POSIXct column holding each row's period. Rows are put in period order within each group, and with panel = "shared" they are matched across groups by period, so the groups may cover different periods. Without index, row t of every group is taken to be the same period, and panel = "shared" needs every group to have the same number of rows.

circular

If TRUE, blocks wrap around from the end of each series to its start (the circular block bootstrap of Politis and Romano, 1992), so every row is equally likely to be drawn. The default FALSE is the moving block bootstrap, which draws the first and last block_length - 1 rows of each series less often than the rest.

cores

Number of cores over which the replicates are evaluated. Values above 1 use parallel::mclapply() on Unix-alikes and a socket cluster elsewhere. Every replicate's rows, and the seed its call to statistic starts from, are drawn in this session before any replicate is evaluated, so the result does not depend on cores. The workers of a socket cluster are new R sessions that load mediamix and nothing else, so there statistic must call other packages with pkg::fun() and must not rely on functions or data defined in your session.

Value

An object of class mm_bootstrap: a data frame with one row per element of the statistic and columns term, estimate (on the original data), lower, upper (percentile interval) and std_error, with the replicate matrix attached as the attribute "replicates" (one row per replicate, one column per term). Replicates in which statistic failed are dropped and counted in a message that quotes the first error. Each term's interval and standard error use the replicates in which that term is finite; missing or infinite values stay in the replicate matrix and are counted per term in a message.

Subsetting the rows keeps the replicate matrix in step with the terms. Removing one of the five columns returns a plain data frame, as do as.data.frame() and, with the broom column names std.error, conf.low and conf.high, tidy().

Details

Transform the media before bootstrapping and put the transformed columns in data. Resampled blocks are glued end to end, so re-running the adstock filter on resampled rows would carry spend across block boundaries that were never adjacent in time; the transformed columns already hold each week's correct carryover.

The interval reflects sampling variation given the model specification, including the transform parameters. It does not include the uncertainty in choosing those parameters unless statistic re-tunes them, which is possible but slow.

Every replicate's rows are drawn before statistic is first called, so a statistic that sets its own seed, as a cross-validated fit often does, cannot make the resamples repeat. Each replicate's call to statistic then starts from a seed drawn for it in advance, which is what makes the replicates the same in a worker process as in this one. Random numbers that statistic draws on the replicates do not advance the caller's stream.

Panels

With by and the default panel = "shared", each replicate draws one set of blocks of periods and takes every group's rows for those periods, the moving blocks bootstrap for panels of Gonçalves (2011). Shocks common to every group, such as a national holiday or a competitor's launch, then stay together, which they must for a statistic pooled across groups. Each group's rows are passed to statistic together, in time order, one group after another.

Groups are matched period by period. With index, a group has no row for a period it does not cover, so group sizes vary from replicate to replicate. Without index, row t of each group is period t, and groups of different lengths are an error: supply index, or use panel = "independent".

With panel = "independent", every group draws its own blocks and keeps its own size. That is only right when the groups share no shocks.

Choosing the block length

A block must be long enough to hold the dependence that matters for the statistic. In media data that is mostly carryover, so a block at least as long as the longest channel's effective_window() is a sensible floor. The default ceiling(n^(1/3)) is a rate rather than a length chosen for the data, and it is often shorter: 6 for 156 weekly rows.

Percentile intervals from a block bootstrap of a short series cover less than their nominal level, and the shortfall grows with the autocorrelation. For the mean of 156 values from an AR(1) process, nominal 90% intervals from 200 replicates covered the true mean in about 81% of 2,000 simulated series when the autocorrelation was 0.5 and blocks were 6 rows long, and in about 71% when it was 0.8, rising to about 75% with blocks of 13 rows. Circular blocks gave much the same figures. Read the intervals as a lower bound on the uncertainty.

The block length is checked against the series it resamples: longer than half the shortest series gives a warning, because few distinct resamples remain, and as long as the series is an error, because every replicate would repeat the data.

References

Gonçalves, S. (2011). The moving blocks bootstrap for panel linear regression models with individual fixed effects. Econometric Theory, 27(5), 1048–1082. doi:10.1017/S0266466610000630

Künsch, H. R. (1989). The jackknife and the bootstrap for general stationary observations. The Annals of Statistics, 17(3), 1217–1241. doi:10.1214/aos/1176347265

Lahiri, S. N. (2003). Resampling Methods for Dependent Data. Springer. doi:10.1007/978-1-4757-3803-2

Politis, D. N. and Romano, J. P. (1992). A circular block-resampling procedure for stationary data. In R. LePage and L. Billard (eds.), Exploring the Limits of Bootstrap, 263–270. Wiley.

See also

plot.mm_bootstrap(), contributions(), roi(), marginal_roi()

Examples

data(mm_weekly)
north <- mm_weekly[mm_weekly$geo == "north", ]
channels <- c("tv", "video", "search", "social", "display")
truth <- attr(mm_weekly, "truth")

# Transform once, on the full series, then bootstrap the model on top.
spec <- lapply(stats::setNames(channels, channels), function(ch) list(
  adstock = list(decay = truth$decay[[ch]]),
  saturation = list(half_max = truth$half_max[[ch]],
                    shape = truth$shape[[ch]])))
media <- transform_plan(north[channels], spec)
names(media) <- paste0(channels, "_t")
d <- cbind(north, media, week = seq_len(nrow(north)))

average_roi <- function(d) {
  fit <- lm(revenue ~ tv_t + video_t + search_t + social_t + display_t +
              week + price + seasonality + holiday, data = d)
  contrib <- colSums(sweep(as.matrix(d[paste0(channels, "_t")]), 2,
                           coef(fit)[paste0(channels, "_t")], `*`))
  stats::setNames(contrib / colSums(d[channels]), channels)
}

boot <- block_bootstrap(d, average_roi, times = 50, block_length = 13,
                        seed = 1)
boot
#> 
#> ── Block bootstrap 
#> 50 replicates, blocks of 13 rows, 90% percentile intervals
#>     term estimate    lower upper std_error
#>       tv    1.310  1.10874 1.882    0.2579
#>    video    1.924  0.01862 3.495    1.1227
#>   search    2.794  1.58295 4.258    0.8991
#>   social    3.614  0.51808 5.213    1.4353
#>  display    1.517 -0.03334 5.217    1.6852

# A panel: every geography takes the same blocks of weeks.
pooled_mean <- function(d) c(revenue = mean(d$revenue))
block_bootstrap(mm_weekly, pooled_mean, times = 50, block_length = 13,
                by = "geo", index = "date", seed = 1)
#> 
#> ── Block bootstrap 
#> 50 replicates, blocks of 13 periods shared across groups, 90% percentile
#> intervals
#>     term estimate lower upper std_error
#>  revenue    26271 25485 26682     370.5
